analysis.one_liner: Expands the federal employees' health insurance model to cover every American without employer or government coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a floor vote, with zero cosponsors, and stalled until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a health insurance program for everyone not covered by Medicare, Medicaid, an employer plan, or other federal programs, run the way Congress and federal workers get coverage. Private insurers could offer plans, but premiums would be community-rated, people with pre-existing conditions could not be denied, and the government would help pay premiums, especially for low-income households. It would be paid for by a payroll-type tax on employers and self-employed people, a tax on hospital revenues, and premiums from enrollees.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured Americans and people whose employers do not offer affordable coverage would get comprehensive insurance modeled on the federal employees' plan, with no pre-existing condition exclusions, community-rated premiums, and subsidies for lower-income households. Small businesses would stop acting as health insurance brokers, since the government would negotiate directly with insurers.

how_it_helps.text: Comprehensive coverage for everyone not already covered, with the same scope of benefits as the federal employees' health program.
No pre-existing condition exclusions and premiums that cannot vary by age, gender, or health status.
Cost-sharing subsidies that bring out-of-pocket costs to zero for low-income individuals, children, and pregnant women.

The government would contribute up to 75 percent of the premium, taking over the job of negotiating rates with insurers, and small businesses would stop having to shop for and administer health plans, which the bill's findings say can eat up over 30 percent overhead for employers with fewer than 10 employees.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and self-employed individuals would pay a new payroll-type tax with rates scaling by firm size and average wages (from 4% to 10%). Hospitals would pay a 2% tax on revenues. Individuals would pay premiums, though subsidized. The government would also keep funding the program through appropriations.

drawbacks.text: Employers would face a new payroll tax even if they already offer coverage, though they could claim a credit to offset it if their coverage met the standard.
Hospitals would pay a new 2% tax on revenues, a cost they might pass on in higher prices or reduce services.

The bill does not include a full public option, so private insurers would remain the channel through which everyone gets coverage, with plans contracted through the government rather than provided by the government itself.
It expands a mandate requiring every uncovered individual to enroll, with default automatic enrollment into a plan if someone does not choose one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's strongest argument is that it builds on a system already working well for federal workers, keeping insurers in the picture but setting clear rules on premiums, pre-existing conditions, and cost-sharing. The trade-off is significant new taxes on employers and hospitals, and it keeps private insurers in the loop rather than creating a government-run plan. It was an early sketch of how to solve uninsuredness with a payroll-financed model.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and then to a health subcommittee, but was never brought to a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in May 2009 with zero cosponsors, the bill was assigned to Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce, then sent to a health subcommittee, and nothing further happened.
The 111th Congress ended in January 2011 without the bill ever receiving a committee vote, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and large employers, in the sense that the payroll tax and hospital tax never became law and insurers were never given a new government-managed contracting role, though the status quo of uninsured Americans also continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo of the uninsured continued

for.name: Rep. James Langevin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and worked to build support, though it attracted no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a floor vote, and no committee action is recorded, so there is no roll-call to show where members stood. Zero cosponsors meant no apparent momentum in either direction.

industries.note: Insurers would gain millions of new enrollees whose premiums are guaranteed and paid partly by the government, and they would be locked in as the only channel for coverage. In exchange they would face community-rated premiums, guaranteed issue, and a 90% medical loss ratio requirement.
Hospitals would pay a new 2% tax on revenues to help fund the program, though they might also gain from fewer uninsured patients they currently treat without compensation.

Employers would pay a new payroll-based tax, scaled by size and average wages, but would stop bearing the administrative burden of shopping for and managing health plans if they shift workers onto the program.
